This is halal french cooking at its most honest — two culinary traditions sharing the same pot. 60 minutes, one dish, real depth. Full recipe on mubashirr.com.

instagram.caption:
Two kitchens, one pot. That is what this tagine is.

On the surface it looks Moroccan — and it is. Preserved lemon, saffron, green olives, beef that has had time to think. But underneath the spice, the logic is French. You build a fond. You sweat aromatics properly. You braise low and slow until the liquid stops being liquid and starts being sauce.

Halal French cooking is not a novelty act. It is just good cooking, applied honestly. No wine standing in for technique. No substitution that quietly apologises for itself. The alcohol was never the point — the patience was.

This recipe takes about 60 minutes start to finish. It works on a weeknight. It works for a table of people you want to impress without performing. The preserved lemon does something to the braising liquid that is difficult to describe before you taste it and obvious the moment you do.

Recipe is on the blog. Link in bio.

email.subject: A tagine built on French logic
email.preheader: Moroccan flavour, French braising discipline. Halal, no alcohol, 60 minutes.
email.body_html:
There is a version of halal cooking that apologises for itself. Recipes that swap wine for grape juice and hope nobody notices. Technique borrowed halfway and then abandoned.

This is not that.

The beef and olive tagine I posted this week is Moroccan in character and French in discipline. You build the base the way a French braise demands — proper fond, sweated aromatics, layered heat. Then you let preserved lemon, saffron, and time do what no shortcut can replicate.

The result is a sauce that is neither substitute nor compromise. It is what the dish always wanted to be, with nothing missing.

A few things worth knowing before you cook it:

  • The preserved lemon is not optional. It does something acidic and floral that no fresh lemon quite matches.
  • Saffron bloomed in warm water, not thrown in dry. The difference is real.
  • 60 minutes is enough. This does not need to be an all-day project.

Halal French cooking is not a genre I invented. It is just what happens when you apply classical technique to ingredients that have always been available to us, without treating the absence of alcohol as a problem to be solved.

Read the full recipe and method here:

Beef and Olive Tagine with Preserved Lemon

linkedin.body:
French cooking and Moroccan cooking have more in common than most people admit.

Both traditions understand that cheap cuts of meat, given patience and proper heat, outperform expensive ones rushed through a pan. Both know that aromatics are not garnish — they are architecture. Both build flavour in stages rather than hoping a sauce covers for what the base lacked.

My beef and olive tagine lives at that intersection. The spice profile is Moroccan: saffron, preserved lemon, cumin, olives that hold their shape through the braise. The technique is French: fond development, controlled sweating, a braising liquid reduced into something that coats rather than pools.

It is also entirely halal. No wine, no substitutes that nudge you toward wine anyway. The dish does not need alcohol to reach depth. It needs time, heat management, and ingredients that earn their place.

I write about halal French cooking because I think the conversation around it is still too narrow. It gets framed as restriction — what you cannot use — rather than as a culinary tradition that is precise, demanding, and genuinely interesting.

This tagine is one example of what that tradition looks like on a plate. Sixty minutes. One pot. Flavour that does not require an explanation.

Recipe is on the blog if you want to cook it this week: https://mubashirr.com/beef-olive-tagine-preserved-lemon-halal-french-cooking/

tweets: French braising technique + Moroccan spice + zero alcohol = a tagine that needs no apology. Here is how it works.

Most halal recipe swaps treat wine as the problem. It is not. The problem is skipping the technique that wine was propping up. Build a proper fond. Sweat your aromatics. Then the liquid you use barely matters.

Preserved lemon does something in a braise that fresh lemon cannot. It is already fermented, already broken down. It does not brighten the dish — it deepens it. Saffron bloomed in warm water does the same thing quietly in the background.

Halal French cooking is not a workaround. It is classical technique applied to ingredients that have always existed. The beef does not know what cuisine it belongs to. It responds to heat, time, and patience — same as it always has.
